title: How to Conduct a Strategy Review
hook: Competitor samples stay boxed while the team rehearses the safest slide in the deck.
counterintuition: A review sounds like progress when the slides are sharp. In fact, it earns its keep only when someone leaves with a changed commitment.
tryThisNow: Before your next review, write three questions: what do we know firsthand, what can we execute, and what changes after this meeting.
keyTakeaway: A strategy review works when its questions sharpen the plan, narrow commitments, and leave behind action that would not have happened otherwise.

breakdown.fastRead:
Frey opens a competitor sample box while the team is still rehearsing slide six. The review can protect the plan, or it can test whether the plan deserves protection.

Run the review so something has to change. Ask what the team knows firsthand. Ask where focus is too wide. Ask what skill is missing and what action will change next. A strong review is not a smarter show. It leaves a sharper plan behind.
breakdown.deepRead:
At 2:36 p.m., Maelle points to five growth ideas on one slide and asks which two the company can actually staff this quarter. A review that cannot force choice becomes a performance.

You can see the mechanism in the first awkward pause. People tend to protect a promise after it has been spoken out loud. They smooth bad news, widen dates, and call vague ownership teamwork. Turning strategy review into a pressure test that produces sharper action cuts through that comfort by asking for the live fact that changes action.

At 7:10 a.m., Tobin brings a customer cancellation email into a review and lays it beside the retention strategy. The useful move is not louder pressure. It is closer contact with the work. Ask who owns the next hard move, what might block it, and what proof will be visible soon. Then stay long enough to change the plan when the answer is rough.

At 4:01 p.m., Ansel writes six action items from a strategy review and realizes none has an owner in the room. There is a limit. Strong execution cannot make a weak premise true. It can only expose the weak premise early, while a leader still has time to change the promise, move the person, narrow the goal, or stop pretending.
breakdown.fullRead:
Frey opens the competitor box during slide six. The team has rehearsed the growth story twice. Nobody has touched the rival sample sitting on the table. The review can continue as a presentation, or it can become a test of what the team actually knows.

The strongest review questions bite into the plan. How well versed is the team about the competition? How strong is the organizational capability to execute? Is the plan scattered or sharply focused? Are these the right ideas, or only attractive ideas? Are the linkages with people and operations clear enough that the strategy can be carried after the meeting?

Bad review habits protect the plan when every question lets the slide survive unchanged. It pressures the plan when a question forces a narrower choice, a new owner, or a different sequence. Maelle makes the theater team choose two audience initiatives because the rehearsal budget cannot carry seven. Vincent pauses a cloud migration review because the database administrator roster has two vacancies. Selene asks operations to stand beside the strategy slide because the linkage cannot be assumed from the wording.

Follow-through is the proof that the review was real. If the room leaves with the same commitments it entered with, the meeting may have sounded intelligent, but the strategy did not get stronger. A good review leaves a shorter action list, a clearer bet, a named capability gap, or a decision to stop doing something that once looked attractive.

There is a skill to keeping the review from becoming hostile theater. The point is not to embarrass the presenters. The point is to make the plan safer by making the weak parts visible while the plan can still change. A good question should be specific enough to require evidence and fair enough that the team can answer without guessing what the leader wants to hear.

What should be different on Monday if the review worked? That question cuts through ceremony. Maybe a competitor comparison is assigned to one person. Maybe a telehealth plan is narrowed to the clinician schedule that can actually hold. Maybe three product ideas become one because engineering weeks are scarce.

The review is management work, not a recital. Ask the question that can change the plan, then make sure the changed plan has someone to carry it.

A review that produces no harder action has mostly reviewed itself.

Useful pressure often feels narrower at the end. Fewer ideas survive, fewer claims remain vague, and fewer owners can hide inside group language. That narrowing is not a loss of ambition. It is the moment ambition starts paying rent in the operating system.

The best leaders also decide what the review is not for. It is not for proving that the team worked hard, defending last month's favorite idea, or letting every unit keep a pet initiative. It is for making the next version of the strategy harder to fool and easier to execute.

examples.title: Frey opens the competitor box during slide six

planSpec.domain: a division president using a competitor sample to interrupt a polished strategy review
planSpec.audience: a leader who needs firsthand competitive knowledge
planSpec.stakes: a plan that may miss a rival's product improvement
planSpec.requiredBeat: he opens the sample instead of letting rehearsed slides carry the review

examples.scenario: At 9:19 a.m., Frey cuts packing tape with a car key while his team rehearses slide six for the strategy review. Inside the box is the rival's new countertop unit, heavier than the photos made it look. The product lead keeps talking about our superior experience. Frey sets the sample on the table with a dull thud. A screw rolls from the packaging. He is about to decide whether the review stays with slides or starts with the thing customers will touch.
examples.whatToDo: Put the competitor's product in the center of the review and ask what the plan changes after seeing it firsthand.
examples.whyItMatters: Strategy review needs real competitive knowledge. A product on the table can expose assumptions a slide would protect.

examples.title: Maelle makes the team choose two growth ideas

planSpec.domain: a strategy review chair forcing focus from five ideas to two
planSpec.audience: a leader whose team has too many appealing ideas
planSpec.stakes: resources spread thin and no idea carried well
planSpec.requiredBeat: she asks which ideas can truly be staffed this quarter

examples.scenario: "They all have merit," the business lead says while Maelle stands beside five growth ideas stacked like a lunch menu. "They all have merit," the business lead says. Maelle uncaps a black marker. "Which two can we staff this quarter without stealing from service recovery?" The room smells like marker and cooling coffee. No one moves. The finance lead looks at the operations lead. Maelle has to decide whether merit is enough to survive the review.
examples.whatToDo: Force the choice in the room. Pick the two ideas with owners, capacity, and economics, then park the rest without pretending they remain active.
examples.whyItMatters: Focus is an execution question. A review that blesses every good idea leaves the organization unable to carry any of them well.

examples.title: Tobin lays the cancellation email beside retention strategy

planSpec.domain: a customer success leader bringing cancellation evidence into a retention review
planSpec.audience: a leader deciding whether rough customer evidence changes strategy
planSpec.stakes: retention spend aimed at the wrong problem
planSpec.requiredBeat: he decides whether a real cancellation email enters the strategy review

examples.scenario: The cancellation email folds once in Tobin's hand before the retention review starts. The strategy slide says loyalty offers will reduce churn. The customer writes that no one fixed the first invoice error after four calls. Tobin can already hear the room saying anecdote. The paper is warm from the printer. He is about to leave it in his folder when the CFO asks whether the retention plan is ready.
examples.whatToDo: Put the email beside the retention slide and ask whether the plan solves the actual reason customers are leaving.
examples.whyItMatters: A review should let rough customer evidence challenge the chosen idea. Otherwise the team funds a fix for the wrong problem.

examples.title: Ansel finds six actions with no room owner

planSpec.domain: a chief of staff reviewing strategy action items with no accountable owners
planSpec.audience: a leader whose review produced notes but not management action
planSpec.stakes: a polished meeting that leaves execution unchanged
planSpec.requiredBeat: she sees that action items without in-room owners made the review hollow

examples.scenario: It takes Ansel six action items and a quiet speakerphone to see that the review assigned no room owner. Every line starts with explore, assess, or revisit. None has a person in the room beside it. The deck was strong. The questions were sharper than last quarter. Still, nothing on the pad can change by Friday. He circles all six verbs and writes owner? so hard the pen tears the paper.
examples.whatToDo: Rewrite each action as a named owner, a decision needed, and a date for proof before the meeting notes go out.
examples.whyItMatters: Follow-through is the test of a review. If the questions do not turn into owned work, the meeting was only a better conversation.

examples.title: Ragna notices the missing rival guarantee

planSpec.domain: a retail executive exposing weak competitor knowledge in a review
planSpec.audience: a leader whose team knows the category but missed the rival's new guarantee
planSpec.stakes: a service promise that may no longer be enough to win
planSpec.requiredBeat: a missing competitor fact changes the review agenda

examples.scenario: What does Ragna's clipped rival guarantee know that the market overview keeps skipping? Before the review, the team sounded confident about delivery speed. After Ragna asks where the guarantee appears in the plan, the room goes still. The marketing lead flips pages. The operations lead whispers that she has not seen the ad. Ragna moves the review from growth story to competitive facts.
examples.whatToDo: Stop the overview and rebuild the review around what the rival changed, what customers now expect, and how the operation can answer.
examples.whyItMatters: A strategy review cannot test a plan against competition it does not know. Missing facts make confident plans brittle.

examples.title: Selene asks operations to stand beside the strategy slide

planSpec.domain: a strategy chief bringing operations capability into the review room
planSpec.audience: a leader who wants strategy, people, and operations linked in the same review
planSpec.stakes: a plan approved without carrying strength
planSpec.requiredBeat: she makes the operations lead name which promise cannot be staffed

examples.scenario: You see Selene's same-day installation slide while the operations lead sits against the wall with no speaking slot. The operations lead is sitting against the wall, silent, with a staffing sheet folded into quarters. Selene asks him to stand beside the slide and mark the cities he can staff by July. He marks seven. The room exhales. Selene feels the old habit, smooth it over and revise later. Instead she lets the seven marks stay visible.
examples.whatToDo: Keep capability in the room. Change the strategy to match staffed reality or make the staffing decision before approval.
examples.whyItMatters: Strategy cannot be reviewed in one room and executed in an imaginary one. Capability has to challenge the plan while choices can still change.

reviewCards.front: A plan sounds clear, but the next hard owner is unnamed. What should you retrieve?
reviewCards.back: Retrieve the execution test: name the owner, the next action, the date, and the evidence that will prove the work moved.

reviewCards.front: A team gives calm status while field evidence feels rough. What move keeps truth close?
reviewCards.back: Ask for the raw signal from the place where the work happens, then decide what changes before the next review.

reviewCards.front: You spot a comforting story covering a weak handoff. What question breaks the spell?
reviewCards.back: Ask what must be true by a near date, who owns that proof, and what will happen if the proof does not appear.

reviewCards.front: A target was built on a false assumption. What does strong follow-through require?
reviewCards.back: Change the target, name the failed premise, and protect the system from pretending the old promise still fits reality.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: turning strategy review into a pressure test that produces sharper action starts with a live promise and forces it into owned action. The habit is to ask what is true now, who owns the next hard move, and what proof will appear soon.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a work plan earns quick agreement, then I will ask for the owner, date, and proof point on the hardest piece before I call it ready.
If I set a health goal, then I will name the next physical setup, the time it happens, and the check I will use tomorrow.
If I keep repeating a personal promise, then I will turn it into one visible action with a time, place, and fallback.
If someone depends on me, then I will state exactly what I will do next and when they can see or hear the result.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within the next 24 hours, choose one promise that sounds settled and write the owner, the next action, the riskiest assumption, and the proof you expect to see within seven days.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: For one week, end each serious planning conversation by asking what changed, who owns the next hard move, and what evidence will be visible before the next check-in.
